blocks.text: Before you can understand Git, you need to understand the more general problem it solves: version control. Git is one implementation of a version control system, but the concept existed long before Git and applies to any project where files change over time.

A version control system (VCS) is software that records changes to a set of files over time, so that you can recall, compare, and restore specific versions later. Instead of a project having exactly one current state that gets overwritten every time someone edits it, a VCS keeps a running history: every meaningful change is captured as a distinct, recoverable point in time.

blocks.title: Assumed baseline today
blocks.content: In modern software engineering, using some form of version control is not treated as optional tooling, it is assumed by default for any real codebase, the same way a text editor or a compiler is assumed. This module builds up from the general concept to exactly why that assumption exists.

blocks.text: 1. The Problem Version Control Solves

Any project that has more than one contributor, or exists across more than one point in time, runs into the same problem: how do you know what changed, when it changed, who changed it, and how do you get back to an earlier state if the current one turns out to be wrong?

Without a system for this, teams fall back on manual, error-prone habits: renaming files with dates or version numbers, emailing attachments back and forth, keeping a folder of backups nobody fully trusts. These habits don't scale past a handful of files or a single person, and they provide no real history, no accountability, and no reliable way to recover a specific past state.

blocks.alt: What a version control system records for every change
blocks.caption: A VCS captures what, who, when, and why for every change, building a full history.

blocks.title: It is not just about code
blocks.content: Version control is a general concept. It applies to source code, but also to configuration files, documentation, design specs, and any other file set that evolves. Git happens to be the VCS almost every software team uses today, but the underlying idea predates it.

blocks.text: 2. A Before/After Scenario

Imagine a small team writing a report in report.doc. Without version control, the common workaround is to manually duplicate the file every time someone wants a safety net: report_v2.doc, then report_v2_final.doc, then report_v2_final_ACTUAL.doc. Nobody can say with confidence which file is current, what changed between any two of them, or who made a given edit.

blocks.alt: Manually managed file copies without version control
blocks.caption: Manual copies pile up with no real history and no clear "current" version.

blocks.text: With a real VCS, the file is tracked instead of duplicated. Every meaningful change becomes a commit: a labeled, timestamped snapshot with a message explaining the change. There is exactly one file on disk, but a full, ordered history behind it that you can inspect or restore from at any point.

blocks.alt: The same project tracked with version control
blocks.caption: One tracked file with a linear, inspectable history of commits instead of scattered copies.

blocks.alt: The structural difference between overwriting and versioning
blocks.caption: Without version control, past states are simply gone; with it, every past state stays reachable.

code.content:
# The manual-copies world (what a VCS replaces)
report.doc
report_v2.doc
report_v2_final.doc
report_v2_final_ACTUAL.doc      # which one is actually current?

# The version-control world: one file, full history behind it
git log --oneline report.doc
# a1b2c3d fix numbers in Q3 section
# 9f8e7d6 add intro paragraph
# 4c3b2a1 initial draft

blocks.title: A familiar smaller-scale analogy
blocks.content: Most people have already used a lightweight form of this idea without calling it version control: a photo editor's undo history, or a document editor's "version history" panel. Both let you step back through past states of one file. A VCS applies the same core idea deliberately, systematically, and across an entire project rather than one file in one app.

blocks.alt: A familiar smaller-scale analogy to version history
blocks.caption: The undo/version history you may have used in a photo or document editor is the same underlying idea as version control.

blocks.text: 3. Why This Matters for Any Project

The need for version control shows up along two independent axes. The first is more than one contributor: as soon as two people can touch the same files, you need a way to track whose change is whose and to combine changes without one person silently overwriting another's work.

blocks.alt: Multiple contributors editing the same project
blocks.caption: Version control tracks each contributor change independently instead of letting one overwrite the other.

blocks.text: The second axis is more than one point in time, even with a single contributor. A solo developer still benefits: you can recall exactly what the code looked like a week ago, compare it to today, and jump back to investigate when a bug was introduced.

blocks.alt: A project timeline with recall points
blocks.caption: Even a single contributor benefits from being able to recall any earlier point in the timeline.

blocks.title: Real scenario
blocks.content: A developer ships a feature, and two weeks later a bug report comes in that the feature seems to have broken something unrelated. Without version control, there is no reliable way to see what the code looked like before the feature landed. With version control, git log and git diff show exactly what changed, when, and by whom, turning a guessing game into a five-minute investigation.

blocks.text: These two axes combine in almost every real project: most software has more than one contributor at some point in its life, and every project, by definition, exists across more than one point in time from the moment it starts. That is why version control is treated as a baseline requirement for software work rather than an optional extra.
4. What a VCS Gives You Beyond Backups

It is tempting to think of version control as "just backups," but a backup only gives you a copy of the current or last-saved state. A VCS gives you every state, indexed and searchable, plus the ability to compare any two of them and understand the difference.

items: Recall: view exactly what a file looked like at any past point.
Compare: see precisely what changed between two points in time.
Restore: bring an earlier version back as the current one, without losing the history in between.
Attribute: know who made a change and, via a commit message, why.

blocks.title: Common pitfall
blocks.content: Relying on cloud file-sync tools (like a shared drive with "version history") is not the same as a real VCS. Those tools usually keep a limited window of recent snapshots with no meaningful commit messages, no way to compare specific versions side by side, and no concept of independent parallel lines of work. Git-style version control is purpose-built for that.

blocks.text: 5. Vocabulary You Will See Everywhere

A handful of terms recur across every version control system, regardless of implementation. Getting comfortable with them now makes every later topic easier, since Git simply gives each of these a concrete mechanism.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Term","Meaning"],"rows":[["Repository","The tracked project itself, plus its full recorded history"],["Snapshot / commit","A single recorded point in the history, capturing the state of the files at that moment"],["History","The ordered sequence of all snapshots from the first to the most recent"],["Diff","The precise difference between two snapshots, showing exactly what changed"],["Restore / checkout","Bringing the files back to how they looked at a specific earlier snapshot"]]}

blocks.title: These apply beyond Git
blocks.content: These terms are not Git-specific. Any real VCS, past or present, needs a way to represent a repository, a snapshot, a history, a diff, and a restore operation. Git's particular answers to each (blobs, commits, the commit graph, tree comparisons, checkout) are covered as this course goes deeper.

blocks.text: 6. Where Git Fits In

Git is a specific, extremely popular implementation of the version control concept described in this topic. It is a distributed VCS, meaning every clone of a project carries the full history, not just a pointer to one central copy. The next topic, Why Version Control, breaks down the concrete practical benefits this unlocks; later topics cover the different flavors of VCS (local, centralized, distributed) and exactly how Git's architecture stores this history.

code.content:
# A first taste of what "tracked, not duplicated" looks like in Git
git init                          # start tracking a project
git add report.doc                 # stage the current state of the file
git commit -m "Initial draft"       # save it as a recoverable point in time
# no report_v2.doc, no report_v2_final.doc -- one file, full history behind it

blocks.text: 7. Version Control at Any Scale

The exact same core model, record changes over time, recall any past version, applies whether the project is a personal weekend script with one contributor or a codebase with thousands of contributors across dozens of teams. What changes with scale is not the underlying idea, only the amount of coordination happening on top of it.

blocks.alt: Version control applies at any project scale
blocks.caption: A solo hobby project and a large-scale codebase rely on the same core model, just with different amounts of coordination on top.

blocks.text: This is worth internalizing early: nothing about version control is inherently "for big teams." A solo developer gets real, immediate value (recall, safe experimentation, disaster recovery) from day one on a brand-new project, well before there is any team to coordinate with at all.

blocks.title: Start using it from commit zero
blocks.content: A common mistake is treating version control as something to "set up later" once a project gets serious. Since the whole value comes from having history, the earlier a project is put under version control, the more of its history is actually recoverable. There is effectively no reason to delay: git init costs nothing and takes seconds.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
points: Version control is a general concept: a system that records changes to files over time so you can recall, compare, and restore specific versions.
It matters for any project with more than one contributor or more than one point in time, which is effectively every real project.
Manually managed file copies break down quickly; a real VCS replaces "which file is current?" with a searchable, attributable history.
Git is one (dominant) implementation of this concept; the next topics build up why it is the standard and how its model actually works.
